title: Muslim neighbors
hook: the Church esteems Muslims who worship the one God (Nostra Aetate 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jewish people, and a pope's name for them. Your line was elder brothers. Who came to mind when you prayed, or simply thought, about your Jewish neighbors? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

Five in the afternoon at a hospital nurses' station. One nurse steps into a supply room, unrolls a small mat, and turns toward the direction she worked out in her first week. Another nurse, a Catholic with a rosary in her scrub pocket, covers the call lights until she's back. Nobody makes a speech. They just know each other's rhythms. The Church has a document that speaks to exactly this kind of neighborliness. It came out of the Second Vatican Council, it's called Nostra Aetate, and it has a short paragraph about Muslims. Today, Muslim neighbors.
screen: `A MAT IN THE SUPPLY ROOM.` → `A ROSARY IN A SCRUB POCKET.` → `ONE SHORT PARAGRAPH.`

segments.voice: The paragraph opens with one word that sets the tone: esteem. The council says the Church regards Muslims with esteem. That is a word for real regard, more than tolerance or politeness. Then it says why, and it does that by naming what Muslims actually do and believe, in terms Muslims would recognize. They worship the one God, living and merciful and all-powerful, the Creator of heaven and earth, who has spoken to humankind. They strive to submit themselves wholeheartedly to God's decrees, the way Abraham submitted, and the council notes that Islam gladly links its faith to Abraham. Next it turns to Jesus and Mary. Muslims, the text says, do not acknowledge Jesus as God, but they revere him as a prophet. They honor Mary, his virgin mother, and at times call on her with devotion. The council doesn't blur the difference about Jesus. It states it plainly, and it still chooses esteem. Then comes the daily life of faith. Muslims await a day of judgment and the raising of the dead. They value the moral life, and they worship God especially through prayer, almsgiving and fasting. Catholics keep those same practices in Lent. Finally the council looks back, honestly. It admits there have been quarrels and hostilities between Christians and Muslims. It asks both to move past that history and to work sincerely for mutual understanding, and together to protect social justice, moral welfare, peace and freedom for everyone. So the paragraph walks a path: esteem, then what is shared, then what differs, then a job to do together. It's a short text, and it fits at a nurses' station.
screen: `THE CHURCH REGARDS MUSLIMS WITH ESTEEM.` · `THE ONE GOD, AND ABRAHAM.` · `JESUS REVERED AS PROPHET; MARY HONORED.` · `PRAYER, ALMS, FASTING, AND A SHARED TASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare to greet a Muslim neighbor. Settle, and breathe. Let one Muslim you actually know, or see often, come to mind. A coworker, a classmate, the family two doors down, the man who runs the corner shop. Recall one thing you know about their day: when they pray, what they're busy with, what they care about. Hold them with esteem for a moment, the council's word. Then choose a simple greeting you'll offer the next time you see them. Hello, and their name, is plenty. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Muslim neighbors. In Nostra Aetate the Church regards them with esteem, as worshipers of the one God who pray, give alms and fast. Today's word.

Your line: with esteem. Today, greet one Muslim neighbor by name, and if a conversation opens, ask one real question about their day and listen to the answer. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching on Muslims draws on the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate, which speaks of esteem. Some parishes and dioceses hold meetings, shared meals or service projects with local mosques.

original.note: Arabic: peace be upon you. the reply wa alaykum as-salam means and upon you be peace.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Church just tolerates other religions.
what it means: Nostra Aetate says the Church regards Muslims with esteem, naming the one God, Abraham, prayer, alms and fasting.
what a scholar hears: the paragraph names shared ground and real difference side by side, then gives both communities a common task.

sources.work: Second Vatican Council, Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions

notes: Nostra Aetate 3 is paraphrased throughout (the Vatican English text is not public domain). Check that the paraphrase of each clause is faithful: esteem; the one God, living, merciful, almighty, Creator, who has spoken; submission like Abraham, with whom Islam links itself; Jesus revered as prophet, not acknowledged as God; Mary honored and at times invoked; day of judgment and resurrection; moral life; prayer, almsgiving, fasting; past quarrels and the call to mutual understanding, social justice, moral welfare, peace and freedom.
The review assumes day 1421 used 'elder brothers' as a pope's phrase for the Jewish people; no year given.
The hospital scene is illustrative; the Muslim nurse's prayer and the Catholic nurse covering for her are invented, not reported.
Original: Arabic greeting as-salamu alaykum and reply wa alaykum as-salam; 'the reply is described as common. Confirm wording and transliteration with an Islam Keeper as well.
